42867374.text: Women with extremely dense breasts have an increased risk of breast cancer but also a decreased sensitivity of mammography. The Dense Tissue and Early Breast Neoplasm Screening (DENSE) trial, initiated in 2011, showed that supplemental full-protocol MRI screening reduced the number of interval cancers in women with extremely dense breasts. Cost-effective screening scenarios have been described, but imaging costs and capacity remain barriers to implementing full-protocol MRI in population-based breast cancer screening programs. Therefore, the DENSE-2 trial was set up to investigate two alternate screening techniques, contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM) or abbreviated MRI (AB-MRI), that are expected to be cheaper and to make more efficient use of the available capacity while potentially achieving similar results to full-protocol MRI. DENSE-2 is a multicenter randomized controlled trial embedded in the Dutch screening program. It comprises two consecutive screening rounds in which women receive the same breast imaging technique both times. The trial investigates the value of supplemental screening with CEM or AB-MRI in women with extremely dense breasts with a negative screening mammogram. The primary aim is to determine whether these methods will lead to a reduction of interval cancers compared with mammography. The DENSE-2 trial results will provide insights into the performance, feasibility, and acceptability of both screening modalities, enable long-term outcome modeling, and support decision-making on the most appropriate screening strategy for women with extremely dense breasts. ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT06636370

42965524.label: Background
42965524.text: Coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) often overestimates stenosis in calcified plaques due to blooming artifacts. The performance of 5.0 T Coronary MR angiography (CMRA) in calcified arteries remains unclear.

42965524.label: Purpose
42965524.text: To assess plaque effects on 5.0 T CMRA image quality and compare diagnostic performance with CCTA.

42965524.label: Population
42965524.text: Forty-six patients with suspected coronary artery disease.

42965524.label: Field strength/sequence
42965524.text: 5.0 T; free-breathing, non-contrast 3D gradient-echo sequence, Dixon water-fat separation, artificial intelligence-assisted compressed sensing.

42965524.label: Assessment
42965524.text: Three blinded radiologists with 6, 8, and 12 years' experience independently evaluated all datasets. Obstructive stenosis was defined as ≥ 50%; CMRA and CCTA image quality used a 4-point scale; quantitative CMRA measures included vessel edge sharpness (VES), signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR). CCTA assessed plaque composition, calcium burden, and calcification length. Invasive angiography was the reference.

42965524.label: Statistical tests
42965524.text: Diagnostic metrics and generalized estimating equations evaluated performance and plaque-image-quality associations. Wilcoxon tests compared visual scores. Agreements used Cohen's κ, Fleiss' κ, and intraclass correlation coefficients.

42965524.label: Results
42965524.text: 5.0 T CMRA showed higher specificity (90.1% vs. 77.7%, p < 0.001) and accuracy (89.4% vs. 82.8%, p = 0.006) than CCTA, with similar sensitivity (88.7% vs. 87.7%, p = 0.740). For CMRA, VES was lower in segments containing mixed plaques than in noncalcified or calcified plaques (16.0 ± 0.8 vs. 18.2 ± 0.8 and 18.3 ± 1.0; p < 0.001). Visual scores differed across calcium-burden categories (3.35 ± 0.07, 3.16 ± 0.09, 2.96 ± 0.09, and 2.79 ± 0.09; p < 0.001). Greater calcification length was associated with lower VES (B = -0.152, p = 0.008) and visual scores (B = -0.019, p = 0.019).

42965524.label: Data conclusion
42965524.text: In this cohort, 5.0 T CMRA showed higher specificity and accuracy than CCTA, with similar sensitivity. Plaque characteristics were associated with selected CMRA image-quality measures.

42986774.text: Gliomas are a heterogeneous group of primary brain tumors that are generally incurable. The current treatment paradigm for these tumors revolves around maximal safe resection and adjuvant chemoradiation; however, posttreatment changes can be difficult to distinguish from residual or recurrent disease. This makes it challenging to know whether treatments are working or the therapy should be escalated. Molecular imaging with amino acid PET has shown promise as a solution to this problem. The authors describe the interpretation considerations for the amino acid radiotracer fluorine 18-fluoroethyltyrosine (FET) in distinguishing posttreatment changes from recurrent glioma. The quantification of FET uptake on PET images and guidelines for interpretation are outlined.

43002574.label: Background
43002574.text: End-stage renal disease (ESRD) increases the risk of myocardial fibrosis. This study aimed to detect cardiac fibroblast activation and fibrosis in ESRD using 18F-labeled fibroblast activation protein inhibitor (FAPI) PET/CT and cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR).

43002574.label: Patients and methods
43002574.text: This prospective clinical trial (NCT07107919) enrolled 33 ESRD patients who underwent 18F-FAPI PET/CT, with 19 patients undergoing CMR. Myocardial FAPI activity was quantified. Cardiac function [left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), right ventricular ejection fraction (RVEF), left atrial ejection fraction (LAEF)] and tissue parameters [native T1, extracellular volume (ECV), late gadolinium enhancement (LGE)] were assessed by CMR. Spearman correlation analysis assessed correlations between 18F-FAPI uptake and CMR parameters.

43002574.label: Results
43002574.text: A total of 75.76% (25/33) of ESRD patients showed myocardial FAPI uptake, significantly higher than the controls (P < 0.05). 18F-FAPI-42 PET identified more segments with evidence of fibroblast activation than CMR-late gadolinium enhancement detected fibrosis (82 vs. 71). Compared with FAPI-negative patients, FAPI-positive patients had increased native-T1, decreased LVEF, LAEF and RVEF (P < 0.05). FAPI-positive segments showed higher native-T1 and extracellular volume % than FAPI-negative segments (P < 0.05). FAPI activity correlated with LVEF, RVEF, LAEF and native-T1. Higher myocardial FAPI uptake was associated with lower LVEF and longer dialysis duration.

43002574.label: Conclusions
43002574.text: 18F-FAPI PET enables in vivo detection of cardiac fibroblast activation in ESRD and correlates with functional and tissue parameters by CMR. FAPI uptake may serve as an imaging biomarker for cardiac remodeling. Further studies are warranted to clarify the role of 18F-FAPI PET in evaluating the efficacy of anti-fibrotic treatment and in assisting cardiac risk stratification in ESRD patients.

43019224.text: A 64-year-old man with treatment-emergent neuroendocrine prostate cancer underwent multitracer PET/CT, which demonstrated low somatostatin receptor expression but marked prostate-specific membrane antigen expression in multiple systemic lesions, including a protruding right abdominal wall metastasis. The patient subsequently received [177Lu]Lu-prostate-specific membrane antigen radioligand therapy combined with olaparib. Follow-up PET/CT showed marked reductions in tracer uptake and tumor burden, accompanied by normalization of the neuron-specific enolase level.

43062624.text: Thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy (TAO), an autoimmune inflammatory disease of the orbit, requires objective assessment of disease activity and severity to guide management. The Clinical Activity Score (CAS) is widely used for this purpose, but its reliability is limited by subjectivity and interobserver variability, and conventional structural imaging cannot reliably distinguish early inflammation from fibrotic remodeling. Orbital single-photon emission computed tomography/computed tomography (SPECT/CT) using 99mTc-DTPA-a small hydrophilic tracer that extravasates in proportion to inflammation-induced microvascular permeability-provides a noninvasive means of visualizing and quantifying orbital inflammatory activity. This review summarizes the imaging principles and quantitative methods of orbital SPECT/CT, from semi-quantitative uptake ratios to corrected SUVmax-based absolute quantification and multiparametric models, and critically appraises the evidence for its clinical applications in TAO activity stratification, prediction of glucocorticoid response, and longitudinal treatment monitoring. Emerging applications, including SPECT/CT radiomics with external validation and artificial intelligence-based image analysis, are also discussed. Throughout, established evidence is distinguished from exploratory applications that require prospective validation, providing a balanced basis for the further evaluation and potential clinical incorporation of orbital SPECT/CT in individualized TAO management.
